entities.name: Rambha

entities.name: Ladha Maharaj
entities.intro: Devotee of Rama from Bileshvar who read the Ramayana to Gandhi's ailing father.

entities.name: Madan Mohan Malaviya
entities.intro: Eminent Hindu scholar and Congress leader.

entities.name: Mavji Dave (Joshiji)
entities.intro: A shrewd, learned Brahman; old friend and adviser of the Gandhi family.

entities.name: Frederic Lely
entities.intro: British Administrator of Porbandar State.

entities.name: Becharji Swami
entities.intro: A Modh Bania turned Jain monk; family adviser.

entities.name: Harilal Gandhi
entities.intro: Gandhi and Kasturbai's eldest son, born 1888 shortly before Gandhi left for England.

entities.name: The caste Sheth
entities.intro: Headman of the Modh Bania caste in Bombay, distantly related to Gandhi.

entities.name: Caste & community
entities.intro: Gandhi belongs to the Modh Bania caste, whose rules forbid crossing the sea.

entities.name: Tryambakrai Mazmudar
entities.intro: A worldly vakil (pleader) from Junagadh who sailed to England with Gandhi to be called to the bar.

entities.name: Dr. P. J. Mehta
entities.intro: Indian doctor in London to whom Gandhi carried an introduction; later a lifelong friend.

entities.name: Dalpatram Shukla
entities.intro: Indian in London to whom Gandhi had an introduction; he helped settle him.

entities.name: Dadabhai Naoroji
entities.intro: The 'Grand Old Man of India', Parsi leader in London and later a British MP.

entities.name: Prince Ranjitsinhji
entities.intro: Kathiawad prince and famous cricketer, one of Gandhi's London introductions.

entities.name: The Richmond friend
entities.intro: An Indian friend of Dr. Mehta (unnamed in the book) who hosted Gandhi in Richmond to teach him English ways.

entities.name: London
entities.intro: Capital of the British Empire, where Gandhi studies law, 1888–91.

entities.name: Bombay
entities.intro: India's great western port city and the centre of law, business and politics.

entities.name: Henry Salt
entities.intro: English writer whose 'Plea for Vegetarianism' converted Gandhi.

entities.name: Dr. Josiah Oldfield
entities.intro: Editor of 'The Vegetarian'; friend of Gandhi in London.

entities.intro: Poet who wrote 'The Light of Asia' and translated the Gita as 'The Song Celestial'.

entities.intro: President of the Vegetarian Society and owner of Thames Iron Works; a puritan.

entities.intro: Author of 'The Ethics of Diet'.

entities.intro: An elderly widow Gandhi met at a Brighton hotel; she became a kind of English mother to him.

entities.intro: London society and weekly paper promoting vegetarianism.

entities.intro: Famous atheist MP, sympathetic to India.

entities.name: Christianity

entities.name: Simple living & economy
entities.intro: Gandhi kept strict accounts and pared down his expenses to live simply.

entities.intro: Gandhi's brief attempt to become polished in English society.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is 16. His father has just died, he is haunted by the 'double shame' of that night, and his first baby has died.
chapters.summary: Gandhi looks back on his religious upbringing. He disliked the pomp of the Vaishnava temple, but his nurse Rambha taught him to repeat Ramanama against fear. A Ramayana reading to his father moved him deeply, and his father's friendships with Jains, Muslims and Parsis taught him tolerance. Missionaries' abuse of Hinduism left him disliking Christianity. Reading Manusmriti pushed him toward atheism, but he became convinced that morality, grounded in truth, is the basis of everything.

updates.rambha: Taught young Gandhi to repeat Ramanama against his fear of ghosts. He credits her with Ramanama becoming 'an infallible remedy' for him.
updates.ladha: His Ramayana readings to the sick Karamchand at Porbandar laid the foundation of Gandhi's devotion to the Ramayana.
updates.malaviya: Mentioned in passing: years later he read the Bhagavat to Gandhi during a 21-day fast.
updates.karamchand: Visited Shiva, Rama and Vaishnava temples, hosted Jain monks, and listened respectfully to Muslim and Parsi friends, giving his son a lesson in tolerance.
updates.religion: Gandhi is tolerant of all faiths but has no living faith yet. He decides that morality is the basis of things and truth its substance. A Gujarati verse teaches him to return good for evil.
updates.christianity: Street missionaries abusing Hindu gods, and gossip that a convert had to eat beef and drink, make the boy dislike Christianity.
updates.truth: 'Truth became my sole objective', and his definition of it keeps widening.
updates.ahimsa: Manusmriti did not yet teach him ahimsa; as a boy he killed insects as a duty.
updates.gita: His father began reading the Gita in his last days.

chapters.situation: Gandhi passes school at 17 and the family, without a father, must decide his future.
chapters.summary: After passing matriculation, Gandhi flounders at Samaldas College in Bhavnagar. Family adviser Mavji Dave urges sending him to England to become a barrister and a future Diwan. His brother agrees to pay, his uncle neither forbids nor helps, and the British administrator Lely brushes him off. His mother consents only after he takes a Jain monk's vow to avoid wine, women and meat.

updates.gandhi: Fails to cope at Samaldas College. Jumps at the idea of England, overcomes his cowardice with a first camel ride to Porbandar, and takes three vows before his mother.
updates.mavjidave: Persuades the family that an English barrister's qualification is the road to a Diwanship and that it will take only three years.
updates.laxmidas: Promises to raise the money for England 'somehow'. Tells Mohandas their father meant him for the bar, not medicine.
updates.tulsidas: Doubts one can stay religious in England but says he will not stand in the way; leaves the decision to the mother.
updates.lely: Tells Gandhi curtly on the staircase to 'pass your B.A. first'; no help.
updates.putlibai: Fears her son will be lost to meat, wine and women in England. Allows him to go only after he takes three vows.
updates.becharji: Administers the vows against wine, women and meat that win Putlibai's consent.
updates.kasturba: Her ornaments are offered to help fund the England trip.
updates.vows: Gandhi swears to his mother not to touch wine, women or meat in England. The vow will be tested repeatedly.
updates.law: The plan is a three-year English bar qualification, expected to lead to a Diwan's post.

status.putlibai: Reluctantly consents to the England trip

chapters.situation: Gandhi has vowed to avoid wine, women and meat and won his family's blessing to study law in England. He sets out for Bombay with his brother.
chapters.summary: Bombay friends advise against sailing in the monsoon, so his brother leaves him there to wait. The Modh Bania caste summons Gandhi and forbids the voyage. When he refuses to obey, the Sheth declares him an outcaste and fines anyone who helps him. His brother stays firm, a friend lends the fare, and Gandhi sails on 4 September 1888 with the Junagadh vakil Mazmudar.

updates.gandhi: Defies the caste meeting calmly and is declared an outcaste. Sails from Bombay on 4 September 1888, aged 18, leaving a wife and baby son behind.
updates.sheth: Orders Gandhi outcasted and fines anyone who helps him or sees him off.
updates.laxmidas: Stands firm against the caste order and confirms his permission by wire.
updates.kasturba: Left behind with a baby of a few months.
updates.harilal: A baby of a few months when his father leaves for England.
updates.mazmudar: Shares Gandhi's cabin on the voyage; promises friends he will look after the 18-year-old.
updates.caste: The Modh Bania caste excommunicates Gandhi for crossing the sea. Even his brother-in-law will not release his money for fear of losing caste.
updates.bombay: Gandhi's departure port, and where the caste confrontation takes place.

status.harilal: Baby, in India with his mother

chapters.situation: Declared an outcaste by his caste, Gandhi has just sailed from Bombay for England, accompanied by the vakil Mazmudar.
chapters.summary: Too shy to speak English or ask which dishes are meatless, Gandhi eats only his own sweets in his cabin. An English passenger insists he will need meat in the cold. He lands at Southampton as the only man in white flannels. In London Dr. P. J. Mehta teaches him etiquette after Gandhi ruffles his top hat. He is homesick and in tears at night, but resolves to finish his three years.

updates.gandhi: Arrives in London in late September 1888. Homesick, starving on tasteless food and anxious about etiquette, but determined to stay three years.
updates.mazmudar: Mixes easily on the voyage and urges Gandhi to talk freely, saying lawyers need 'a long tongue'.
updates.pjmehta: Meets Gandhi on his first evening in London, scolds him for stroking his top hat the wrong way, and teaches him English manners.
updates.dadabhai: One of the four people Gandhi carries introductions to.
updates.ranjitsinhji: One of Gandhi's four letters of introduction.
updates.shukla: One of Gandhi's four letters of introduction.
updates.diet: On board Gandhi lives on his own sweets and fruit. Told he cannot survive England without meat, he says he would rather go home.
updates.vows: Holds to his vow at sea even when warned England is too cold to live without meat.
updates.london: Gandhi arrives at the Victoria Hotel, is shocked by a £3 bill, and moves into rooms found by a Sindhi friend.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has just arrived in London, homesick and half-starved, coached by Dr. Mehta in English manners.
chapters.summary: Dr. Mehta sends Gandhi to live with a friend in Richmond to learn English ways. The friend argues endlessly that he must eat meat, even reading him Bentham, but Gandhi refuses to break his vow. Moved to a widow's house in West Kensington, he walks miles looking for food. He finds a vegetarian restaurant in Farringdon Street and buys Salt's 'Plea for Vegetarianism'. He becomes a vegetarian by choice, and spreading vegetarianism becomes his mission.

updates.gandhi: Becomes a convinced vegetarian after reading Salt. Takes up newspaper reading and walks ten to twelve miles a day.
updates.richmondfriend: Hosts Gandhi for a month, treats him like a brother and argues constantly for meat. Gives up after Gandhi says 'a vow is a vow'.
updates.pjmehta: Moves Gandhi in with a friend and then a family to learn English life.
updates.shukla: Places Gandhi with an Anglo-Indian widow in West Kensington and gets him reading newspapers.
updates.salt: His 'Plea for Vegetarianism', bought for a shilling, converts Gandhi to vegetarianism by conviction.
updates.rambha: Gandhi credits the faith Rambha planted for his daily prayers while resisting meat in London.
updates.diet: The turning point: from vegetarian by obedience to vegetarian by choice. Spreading vegetarianism becomes his mission.
updates.vows: The Richmond friend calls a vow made 'before an illiterate mother' superstition, but Gandhi holds firm.

chapters.situation: Newly converted to vegetarianism by Salt's book, Gandhi still worries his Indian friend, who fears he will never fit in.
chapters.summary: Gandhi reads Howard Williams, Anna Kingsford and Allinson on diet. When he asks a waiter whether the soup is vegetarian, his friend sends him out of the Holborn Restaurant. To compensate, Gandhi tries to become an English gentleman with a Bond Street suit, top hat, and lessons in dancing, violin, French and elocution. After about three months he realises it is folly and becomes a serious student.

updates.gandhi: Spends about three months on clothes, dancing, violin and elocution, then quits all of it and turns to study. His care over dress lasts for years.
updates.richmondfriend: Makes a last attempt at the Holborn Restaurant and banishes Gandhi from the table over the soup. They stay friends.
updates.laxmidas: Sends his brother a double gold watch-chain at his request.
updates.howard: Gandhi reads 'The Ethics of Diet', which claims famous sages were vegetarian.
updates.allinson: Gandhi finds his writings on diet-based healing very helpful.
updates.englandgent: Top hat, evening suit and lessons in dance, violin and elocution, then a sudden awakening and abandonment.
updates.diet: Dietetic experiments become central to his life, at first for health and later for religion.

status.gandhi: London law student, giving up gentlemanly pretensions

chapters.situation: Gandhi has dropped his attempt to become an English gentleman and resolved to be a serious student.
chapters.summary: Gandhi accounts for every farthing and halves his costs by renting his own rooms and walking everywhere. Ashamed of the burden on his brother, he moves into one room, cooks porridge and cocoa, and lives on a shilling and threepence a day. He fails Latin in the London Matriculation, tries again, and passes.

updates.gandhi: Lives on 1s 3d a day in a single room and walks eight to ten miles daily. Passes the London Matriculation on the second attempt, after failing Latin.
updates.laxmidas: Keeps sending money; Gandhi is pained by how much his brother struggles to support him.
updates.lely: His snub ('graduate first') still stings and spurs Gandhi to take the London Matriculation.
updates.simplicity: The habit of strict accounts starts here and stays with him for life. Simple living makes his life feel 'more truthful'.

status.gandhi: Frugal student in a single room, passed London Matriculation

chapters.situation: Gandhi now lives very frugally on porridge and cocoa and has passed his London Matriculation.
chapters.summary: Gandhi joins the Vegetarian Society, sits on its Executive Committee, and experiments with dropping condiments, tea and starch. He briefly eats eggs, then gives them up after deciding his mother's definition of meat included them. He works out a rule for interpreting vows: accept the meaning intended by whoever administered them. He starts a short-lived vegetarian club in Bayswater with Sir Edwin Arnold as Vice-President.

updates.gandhi: On the Vegetarian Society's Executive Committee; founds and runs as Secretary a short-lived Bayswater vegetarian club, his first organizing experience.
updates.putlibai: Her understanding of 'meat', which includes eggs, binds her son's vow.
updates.oldfield: President of Gandhi's Bayswater vegetarian club.
updates.arnold: Agrees to be Vice-President of the Bayswater vegetarian club.
updates.vegsociety: Gandhi joins, subscribes to its weekly and is soon on the Executive Committee.
updates.diet: Gives up condiments, tea and coffee, and eggs. Learns that 'the real seat of taste' is the mind, not the tongue.
updates.vows: Golden rule of vows: honour the meaning given by the one who administered the pledge, or the weaker party's meaning.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is now an active member of London's vegetarian movement, though still tongue-tied in meetings.
chapters.summary: Called 'a drone' by Dr. Oldfield for never speaking, Gandhi writes out his view when the committee moves to expel Dr. Allinson for advocating birth control. He argues that Allinson's moral views are irrelevant to a vegetarian society, but cannot read it aloud. His side loses. He also fails to deliver speeches at Ventnor and at his own farewell dinner. He concludes that his shyness taught him economy of words and served truth.

updates.gandhi: Defends Allinson's right to membership even though he disagrees with him. Breaks down during every attempted speech in England.
updates.oldfield: Teases Gandhi as a 'drone' for never speaking at committee meetings.
updates.allinson: Expelled from the Vegetarian Society committee for advocating birth control, despite Gandhi's written objection.
updates.hills: Moves to expel Allinson; Gandhi respects him but thinks the move improper.
updates.howard: Invites Gandhi to speak at Ventnor; Mazmudar has to read Gandhi's speech for him.
updates.mazmudar: Reads Gandhi's speech for him at Ventnor and gives an applauded speech of his own.
updates.shyness: Gandhi can't speak even from a script. He later sees his shyness as a shield that taught him to measure his words.
updates.vegsociety: Splits over Allinson's expulsion; Gandhi is on the losing side and probably resigns from the committee.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is still shy but increasingly at home in London's vegetarian circles.
chapters.summary: Like other Indian students, Gandhi passes himself off as a bachelor although he is married with a son. A kindly Brighton widow invites him to dinner every Sunday and seems to be steering him toward a young lady. He confesses in a carefully drafted letter that he is married, and she replies with laughter and keeps inviting him.

updates.gandhi: Pretends to be single, then confesses by letter that he is married and a father, and never hides it again.
updates.brightonlady: Helps Gandhi with a French menu, hosts him on Sundays and introduces him to young women. On learning he is married she laughs and remains a friend.
updates.kasturba: Gandhi conceals his marriage in England for a time, then admits it.
updates.harilal: Gandhi admits in his confession letter that he is 'the father of a son'.
updates.truth: Gandhi rids himself of 'the canker of untruth' by confessing his marriage.
updates.childmarriage: Indian students in England hide their child marriages out of shame.

chapters.situation: Having confessed that he is married, Gandhi turns in his second year to questions of religion.
chapters.summary: Two Theosophist brothers introduce Gandhi to the Gita in Arnold's 'Song Celestial' and to 'The Light of Asia', and take him to meet Madame Blavatsky and Annie Besant. He declines to join the Theosophists. A Christian vegetarian gives him a Bible: the Old Testament bores him, but the Sermon on the Mount 'went straight to my heart'. He reads Carlyle on the Prophet and attends Bradlaugh's funeral, which hardens his rejection of atheism.

updates.gandhi: Reads the Gita for the first time, in English, with Theosophists. Is moved by the Sermon on the Mount, and tries to reconcile the Gita, The Light of Asia and the Sermon.
updates.arnold: His Gita translation, 'The Song Celestial', and 'The Light of Asia' become Gandhi's entry into Hindu and Buddhist scripture.
updates.besant: Gandhi meets her at the Blavatsky Lodge just after she has joined the Theosophists.
updates.bradlaugh: Dies; Gandhi attends his funeral with other London Indians.
updates.theosophy: The Theosophist brothers introduce Gandhi to the Gita and Blavatsky. He declines to join, but they make him want to study Hinduism.
updates.gita: First reading, in Arnold's translation, with the Theosophists. The verses on desire leading to ruin strike him deeply. He later calls it the book 'par excellence' for knowledge of Truth.
updates.christianity: A Manchester Christian corrects his Rajkot prejudices. The Sermon on the Mount's 'turn the other cheek' delights him and recalls the verse about returning good for evil.
updates.religion: Gandhi resolves to study all the major religions and comes to see renunciation as the highest form of religion.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has begun reading the Gita and the Bible in London, but his religious knowledge has not yet been tested.
chapters.summary: At a vegetarian conference in Portsmouth, Gandhi and a friend lodge in a house of loose reputation. Over bridge, indecent jokes draw him in until his companion warns him to leave. He flees to his room shaking and quits Portsmouth the next day. He reflects that religious knowledge is useless in a crisis and that only prayer and God's help saved him.

updates.gandhi: Nearly succumbs to temptation in Portsmouth at 20, the first time a woman other than his wife moves him to lust. Leaves the town the next day.
updates.vows: The vow against women holds at Portsmouth, thanks to a friend's warning.
updates.brahmacharya: Gandhi's first real trial in England. He credits God, not his own will.
updates.religion: Gandhi realizes that religious knowledge is 'chaff' compared with experience, and calls prayer more real than eating or walking.
